author: blu
body: An applied effect op performed OUTSIDE the function that installed its handler. Inside that function the clause emission parks the op name in a local and emit-indirect-call takes it; every other function reaches the SAME clause through the handler table, which is global state at runtime -- that dynamic reach is the whole point of the table. Until the FileSystem layer no program performed an op outside the handler's own body, so this path emitted a direct call by name and died at finalize with CDX2040. The op-table walk is gated on user-arity < 0, so an ordinary call never pays it; a constructor application skips it by matching its tag first.

author: blu
body: "Over locals" is a hard requirement on BOTH operands, and the reason is the ordering above rather than the emission. The order is computed by tco-arg-reads, which reports which parameters an argument reads, and it can only see through a name -- give it a field access, a call or any other shape and it answers "reads nothing", so the planner believes that argument is safe to schedule after the parameters it actually depends on have been overwritten.

author: blu
body: is-direct-tail-binop used to accept ANY left operand when the right was a small literal and the operator was add or sub. That is how `s.v + 1` came to be written from a parameter slot that the argument before it had already replaced: a wrong number, silently, with no diagnostic and no fault. Widening the direct shapes therefore means teaching tco-arg-reads to see the new shape FIRST; the two are one change, never two. Pinned by codex/test/tco-direct-arg-reads.

author: blu
body: The shuffle verifier. The planner above decides an order and has always been trusted to have decided it correctly; nothing checked the order it produced, and two miscompiles have shipped out of this code. The checks below are stated over the plan the emitter is about to use, not over the search that built it, so a defect in the search is visible to them. CDX9006, CDX9007 and CDX9008 stand on the LIR emission path and cannot reach here, and the tree emitter is what handles most of every compile.

author: blu
body: The first is that acceptance implies analysis. is-direct-tail-arg decides which arguments are written straight into their parameter; tco-arg-reads decides what those arguments read; the ordering is sound only while the second sees everything the first admits. It has been wrong once. is-direct-tail-binop accepted any left operand at all when the right was a small literal, tco-arg-reads walks only names, and `s.v + 1` was therefore scheduled after the parameter `s` had already been overwritten -- a wrong number, silently. tco-reads-visible answers True for exactly the shapes tco-arg-reads can see through, so widening one without the other is a halt instead.

author: blu
body: The second is the ordering itself: no direct argument may be written after a parameter it reads has been replaced. An argument reading its own target is fine, because that read and that write are the same instruction, and it cannot appear in the written set anyway. The complex arguments do not participate: they are evaluated into temps before any parameter is written and copied out after.

author: blu
body: Load any local straight into target. For a register-local this is a plain mov (elided when already in target); for a spilled local it is a single mov from the frame slot. Unlike load-local it needs no scratch and leaves the load-local toggle untouched -- the caller has named the destination, so there is nothing transient to rotate.

author: blu
body: The lesson for the next person here: this hole was invisible from every direction the instrument could look at itself. The always-on self-test passes because PmTestRec is a record; a zero escape count reads as a clean phase; and the constructor whose fields were lost still reported its own name. Ask what a walk is not visiting before reading its silence as agreement.

author: blu
body: So the offset is computed in place from the field already in hand, which also skips `find-target-type`'s scan for a type `f.type-val` already is. If you add anything to this walk, check R10 across it before and after.

author: blu
body: `return-type` is emitted faithfully rather than as a zero. The walk does not read it, but a null in a `List` slot is a fault waiting for the first reader that does, and the honest list is two words.

author: blu
body: The failure is quiet in both directions, which is why it lasted: the self-test passes (PmTestRec is a root), and a phase whose root is missing looks like a phase with nothing to report. When adding a precise root at a call site, add its type here in the same change and confirm the count moves off zero against a deliberately-wide range before trusting a zero against the real one.

author: blu
body: `extra-patches` is where the second test goes. Everything that reports one patch reports an empty list here, and the branch emitter patches the head and the tail to the same landing site.

author: blu
body: Every field test a pattern emitted lands where its tag test lands: the next branch. They are patched to the same target as next-branch-patch, which is the code position reached once this branch's body and its jump-to-end have been written.
